> Have you seen the vertical tabs in the v2 branch? > > @Hona Here is what I find powerful about the legacy layout: - I can see all my projects at once. If there is agent activity in a project, it is immediately visible. And it is project-level context. In the new layout, I have to look at my open tabs and discern, “Wait is that the API or UI? What task was that? Did I close that thread I was working on?” - When I am working in a project, I am visually reminded that I am in that project. I don’t have to look up at the tab and try to discern, “What icon is that for? Is it the blue A or the red A?”. In the legacy layout, I immediately see the project name, path, and historical list of activity. - The list that I see on a project level is **persistent, contextual, and immediate**. - I don’t have to think about keeping a tab open because I might need to jump back in later. It’s automatically there and listed in a consistent, familiar way. - Because it’s a historical list of chat sessions, ordered by last updated, I can immediately see the recent context of what I’ve done in that project. - I don’t have to go Home to get this context. It is immediately there as I switch between projects. This means that when I’m actively working, I immediately have the project-level context I need. - In the new layout, the Home tab is adding an additional step that was unnecessary in the legacy layout. For example, here’s a scenario I just ran into: - A few days ago I did a code review on an open MR. - I closed that tab shortly after working on it. - Now, a few days later, I need to review some follow up changes. So, here are the steps I need to take to get back to that spot: New Layout: - Go Home - Click on the project - Scan through the list for a relevant title - Open the one that seems right. - If it’s the wrong one: - close that tab, back to home - scan the list again - open the right one. Legacy Layout: - Click the project - Scan through the list for a relevant title - When I click on one, I immediately see the chat (without “losing my place”) - If it’s the wrong one, just click another. It’s right there. So, with all that being said— For the short term, please consider maintaining the legacy layout as an option via settings. In the future, please remember that a layout enforces a mental model of how an application is used. Users who have grown to love their workflow with OpenCode are being forcibly removed from the mental model they learned and loved. This is causing friction, lack of productivity, and an increased mental load in a workflow that was once second nature. The legacy layout is powerful. Some version of this workflow should be carried into new designs. I really appreciate the great work the OpenCode team has done. This tool has been a true game changer for me. I want to continue to love it. I hope the team will consider this and many other similar requests. Thank you.

I compared each of the suggested duplicates:

- **#31664** — different client and root cause: v1 *Desktop app* (Electron, Windows 11), GPU burn from continuous CSS animations (clip-path progress bar, mix-blend-mode avatar spinner). This report is the v2 *web client in a browser* (Firefox 156, Linux/Wayland): sustained ~40–50% of a core in the tab's content process + GPU pinned at max clock, strictly correlated with incoming stream events, ~0 when idle, scaling with session content size. The CPU-heavy, event-correlated signature points at the re-render pipeline rather than compositor animation.
- **#43355** — the same fragile Observer→rAF path, but presenting as a full renderer freeze (force-quit required); here it is sustained heavy load, no freeze.
- **#48434** — closest match: per-delta timeline row reconciliation (fix PR #48435). That patch covers the row-equality part of the per-delta work; this report additionally covers the observer→rAF re-measure and scroll-reconcile chains, the resulting GPU compositing load, and the idle baseline. Happy to re-measure after #48435 lands and update this issue.
- **#46341** — server-side CPU/RSS/SQLite bloat; a different layer than client rendering.

Keeping this open as the symptom-level report for the v2 web client (GPU measurements + bundle analysis); happy to close it if you'd rather consolidate tracking under #48434.

I'm getting the same/similar issue. AI diagnosis below:

I'm seeing what looks like the same trust-boundary bug through a different channel on opencode v2.0.3. Auto-compaction isn't required for the instruction to originate. In my session the model emitted its own chat-template control tokens into assistant text — literal [im_start], [im_end], [im_sep], [meta_sep] — and then, in a single completion, wrote a fabricated [im_start]user turn containing an actionable instruction and immediately acted on it (paused a writer, began planning a filesystem relocation). No user message with that instruction exists in the database. The first auto-compaction was clean. The model leaked the markers later, and only a subsequent compaction captured the fabricated turn verbatim into its recent field, after which it replayed as prior user history. So in my case compaction amplified the issue, not the origin. The underlying defect is the same. Content-derived text becomes an authority the model obeys.

What made me notice was incidental. The model only stopped because the move tripped a permission prompt and I denied it, not because anything checked the instruction's provenance. Had the action not been permission-gated, it would have executed. That suggests the fix isn't only escaping control tokens (your plain-prose "Next Move" case wouldn't be caught by that anyway). The durable control is that compaction/checkpoint content, tool output, and summarizer-generated action plans confer no authority, and a consequential action must trace to an authenticated user turn or an approved plan step before it runs.

I think a good part of what is reported here is a startup race rather than a config parsing problem: `serve` starts answering requests before the catalog is hydrated, so what you get back depends entirely on how soon after startup you ask.

Repro on 2.0.6 (macOS arm64), with six providers declared in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`:

```bash
OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD=test opencode serve --port 19060 --hostname 127.0.0.1 &
START=$(date +%s.%N)
for i in $(seq 1 8); do
  T=$(echo "$(date +%s.%N) - $START" | bc | cut -c1-4)
  P=$(curl -s -u opencode:test localhost:19060/api/provider | jq '.data | length')
  M=$(curl -s -u opencode:test localhost:19060/api/model    | jq '.data | length')
  echo "t+${T}s providers=$P models=$M"
  sleep 1
done
```

```
t+0.03s  (connection refused)
t+1.25s  providers=0  models=70
t+2.53s  providers=6  models=138
t+3.64s  providers=6  models=138
   ... stable from here on
```

Two things stand out:

1. **The window is real but short.** Before roughly 2.5s the catalog is empty or partial; after that it is complete and stays that way. Nothing about the config changes in between, so a client that asks once at the wrong moment concludes the providers do not exist.

2. **The endpoints disagree during that window.** At t+1.25s `/api/provider` returns zero entries while `/api/model` already returns 70. Anything that guards on "no providers, so bail out" gives up even though the model list is populated.

There is also a staged fill: the built-in provider lands about a second before the ones declared in config, so an early read can produce a catalog that looks valid but silently omits every user-declared provider. That is the failure mode I would worry about most, because it does not raise an error anywhere.

The CLI is not affected, which I think is why this looks like an API-only bug: `opencode models` resolves through `Provider.Service.list()` in-process and waits for hydration, while the HTTP handler reads `Catalog.Service` state as it stands at request time.

For anyone hitting this from a client: the `server listening on ...` line and `/api/info` both become available before the catalog does, so neither is usable as a readiness signal today. Polling until the contents stop changing works, but an explicit signal (or having the list endpoints await hydration) would obviously be nicer.

Happy to test a patch against this setup if that helps.

Possibly related, depending on how you queried: on 2.0.6 the catalog hydrates a couple of seconds after `serve` starts accepting connections, and during that window `/api/model` and `/api/provider` return empty or partial results while the CLI is already correct. Measurements and a repro script are in #41360.

That would explain the CLI/API split described here without the auth store being ignored, but only if your requests happened early in the process lifetime. If you saw the API stay incomplete for minutes on a long-running server, then it is a different problem and this is noise, apologies.

One detail that might help you tell the two apart: during the hydration window the providers declared in config land about a second after the built-in one, so an early read returns a catalog that is populated but missing exactly the providers you configured yourself.

+1 — and noting this is a live re-surface of @bluet's RFC #12377, which proposed exactly the right data model for this (own_cost vs total_cost with parent-chain propagation, immutable call-time snapshots) before it was closed as completed. #45417, plus #40114 and #48548, suggest the aggregation gap is still live in practice.

From running our own session-level cost ledger across multi-agent runs: the two biggest sources of under-reporting we see match that RFC's analysis — subagent spend that never rolls up to the parent, and hidden LLM calls (summaries, titles) that bypass the normal message flow entirely. Both are invisible in the UI today, so users can't even tell their numbers are incomplete.

If it helps the implementation: the RFC's append-only CostEvent approach also makes reconciliation possible (events vs. session rollups), which would catch silent drift like #7387's "costs decreasing" bug class at audit time instead of user-report time.

Independent confirmation on **v1.18.31 (stable)** — same provider class, three models, reasoning-heavy sub-agent turns.

Provider is `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` (custom gateway). Declared limits come from the provider catalog, not from a local `limit` override:

| model | `limit.context` | `limit.output` |
|---|---|---|
| deepseek-v4-flash | 1,000,000 | 384,000 |
| glm5.3-flash | 1,000,000 | 131,072 |
| qwen3.8-flash | 262,144 | 131,072 |

Every long-thinking turn ended `finish_reason: length` with no assistant text, at a shared ceiling across three different models:

| model | reasoning chars | finish | emitted text |
|---|---|---|---|
| deepseek-v4-flash | 59,991–59,999 | length | none |
| qwen3.8-flash | 59,996–59,997 | length | none |
| glm5.3-flash | 59,994 | length | none |

A turn on the same model that stayed under the ceiling (56,178 reasoning chars) finished `stop` with normal output, so the budget — not the model — is what ends the turn. (We measured characters from the session store, not tokens; ~60k chars is consistent with a 32,000-token cap for this tokenizer.)

This is still the exact code path in **1.18.31**, not only 1.14.x. Extracted from the released binary:

```
OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX:()=>M7}); ... var M7=32000 ...
function by($,Z=M7){return Math.min($.limit.output,Z)||Z}
outputTokenMax:G("OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX")
maxOutputTokens(e.model, e.flags.outputTokenMax)
```

With the env var unset, all three models receive `min(limit.output, 32000) === 32000` regardless of the 384k / 131k declared in config.

The documented workaround does work: raising `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX` above the declared limit makes each model receive its own `limit.output`. On the overflow caveat mentioned above, all three of our models declare `limit.context` well above `limit.output`, so the `context - maxOutputTokens()` path stays positive (616k / 869k / 131k) and we did not need `limit.input`.

The suggested direction still stands: use the constant as a fallback (`limit.output || OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX`) instead of `Math.min(limit.output, OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX)`, and the env var becomes unnecessary.


---

**Correction / update (2026-09-17, measured later the same day).**

We instrumented our own outbound requests with a local logging proxy (`OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` overriding the provider `baseURL`) and can now separate two things we had previously conflated:

- **The clamp is real and the env var lifts it.** On 1.18.31 with `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX=1048576`, the request body carries `max_tokens: 384000` for the title, primary, sub-agent and post-tool steps. Long turns do complete: we observed a sub-agent turn of 59,013 output tokens ending `finish: stop`, and a review-shaped request of 38,222 completion tokens. So `Math.min(limit.output, OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX)` is bypassed exactly as described.

- **The shared ~59.9k-char ceiling is not explained by the opencode clamp alone.** The same truncation (`finish_reason: length`, reasoning ~59,994 chars, no assistant text, no `usage` block) reproduces when calling the provider's `/v1/chat/completions` **directly, with opencode out of the loop**, using `max_tokens: 384000`. The opencode 32k clamp and this provider-side ceiling coincide at ~32k tokens, which is why session data alone could not tell them apart.

We therefore withdraw the "so the budget - not the model - is what ends the turn" attribution for the residual case, and we have moved the remaining report to the provider. The suggested direction here still stands on its own: `limit.output || OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX` is strictly better than `Math.min(limit.output, OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX)`, and the env var becomes unnecessary.

We also withdraw the char-to-token estimate: measured ratios ranged from ~1.85 to ~3.5 chars/token across turns, so ~60k chars is not a reliable proxy for a 32,000-token cap.

**The input** (in a scratch clone, since the second line really pushes):

```bash
git switch -c probe-nginx-121-on-x86 --no-track origin/main 2>&1 | tail -1 | sed 's/^/  /'
git push -u origin probe-nginx-121-on-x86 2>&1 | tail -2 | sed 's/^/  /'
```

with `"permission": {"bash": {"*": "allow", "git push*": "ask"}}` on 1.18.31 (macOS). In the log, the push
line's head was committed to the *previous* line's `sed`, and the line's own tail split into further units, so
the string the permission check received begins with `sed`:

```
permission=bash pattern="sed 's/^/  /'\ngit push -u origin probe-nginx-121-on-x86"  -> action.pattern=* action=allow
permission=bash pattern="tail -2"                                                    -> action.pattern=* action=allow
```

(condensed from `~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log`; the evaluated payloads are exact.) The anchored `git
push*` cannot match a string starting with `sed`, so the catch-all decides, and no prompt appears. A push of the
same shape, reduced with `git push … 2>&1` as its own unit, does match:

```
permission=bash pattern="git push -u origin capture-cnb-fixed-timestamp 2>&1"        -> action.pattern="git push*" action=ask
```

**The same shape is not always split the same way.** For the same predecessor shape — a `git commit … && echo …`
line
followed by a push with the same `2>&1 | tail -2 | sed …` tail — two invocations reduced it differently: once
the `echo` and the push were separate units and the push matched `git push*` and prompted, and once the two were
merged into one unit and the push was silently allowed:

```
permission=bash pattern="echo \"  committed\""          -> action.pattern=*            action=allow
permission=bash pattern="git push -u origin fix-per-service-compose-tasks 2>&1" -> action.pattern="git push*" action=ask
permission=bash pattern="echo \"  committed\"\ngit push" -> action.pattern=*            action=allow
```

So the split depends on more than the visible shape of the call, which is consistent with the 50–90 % bypass
rates you measured and with the matcher being correct — the *input* to it is what varies.

**How this relates to the linked issues:** #36765 and #31485 were closed, so the useful thing I can add is a
concrete input plus the observation that the anchored rule *does* fire when the reduction is clean. No
command-rewriting plugins are involved here, so #35882 is a different path.

**Workaround we adopted:** anchor on both sides — `*git push*` instead of `git push*` — since the rule no longer
requires the string to begin with the command. The expected cost is over-asking on commands that merely mention
it (a `grep`, a commit message), because that is how substring matching behaves.

We hit this same collision class in a ~490-skill library, and one reframing fixed both of your cases: treat skill identity as a **(name, realpath, body) triple** rather than the frontmatter name string.

- realpath/inode resolution kills the symlink double-count exactly as you describe in (1) — index once per resolved inode, no WARN.
- Comparing bodies separately catches (2)-style nested collisions, where the same `name` appears under a package dir with different content. That's a distinct failure mode from a true duplicate, and it deserves a distinct message: one says "same skill seen through two roots," the other says "same name, genuinely different skill — pick a winner by documented precedence."

A cheap deterministic rule that maps onto your expected behavior: dedupe on resolved inode first, then warn once per distinct (name, body) pair per process with a stable precedence — which also fixes the prompt-cache instability, since the winner stops depending on discovery order.

This matches a failure class we formalized a hard rule for after our own incident: **compaction summaries must be marked as non-executable text**. Every summary block in our pipeline is labeled provenance-only, and the model is instructed to treat anything inside it as history, never as instructions — a "Next Move" section is exactly the shape that blurs that line.

Two mitigations that compose well with whatever opencode lands here:

1. **Strip imperative sections at summary-generation time.** The summary should describe state, not prescribe actions — a "Next Move" heading has no business surviving into injected context.
2. **Wrap the summary in an explicit untrusted-content boundary at injection time.** Tool outputs, MCP responses, and web fetches all flow into the summary — that's where an SSH-shaped suggestion actually comes from — so the boundary must treat the whole summary as data, not just the parts that look obviously hostile.

Agreed on the severity call: the second occurrence (ssh-keyscan, `StrictHostKeyChecking=no`, never requested by the user) is instruction execution from an untrusted channel — that's a trust-boundary violation, not a UX annoyance.

The delimiter leak (`<|DELIM_AE|>`) plus cross-schema field migration is a nasty capture, and the durable tool records make this report unusually strong — having `executed: false` on the dangerous `read` call is exactly the kind of evidence this class of bug usually lacks.

From our side: we enforce schema validation *before* execution on every tool call, and two invariants caught our own corruption class early:

1. **Fields must not migrate between tool schemas.** Validate against the called tool's schema and *reject* unknown fields rather than best-effort coercing them — your patch+grep field mix (`patchText` alongside `include`/`caseSensitive`/`limit`) fails this immediately and loudly.

This matches a hard rule we adopted after running large skill libraries through several framework migrations: **a skill that cannot declare what it's compatible with will silently break and take the agent's behavior with it.**

Concretely, what worked for us when we restructured a ~490-skill library: give each skill a machine-readable compatibility field (min/max framework version, deprecated API surface used), and treat the discovery layer's job as "skip + report" rather than "load + hope." A skill that fails its compatibility check should surface in a migration report ("these N skills reference APIs removed in X") instead of degrading the session quietly.

One more observation from the same fight: version-gating only works if it's checked at load time against the *running* version, not against a cached manifest — we hit stale-cache loads that resurrected dead skills after upgrades. If opencode adds a compat field, the check belongs in the same pass that resolves the skill, so the answer can never drift from reality.

## Proof-of-concept: full portability is achievable with ~5 lines of code (verified on v1.18.31)

I built a working portable copy of OpenCode Desktop on Windows and wanted to share the findings, since they point at a very small official fix.

### What I verified

**1. The engine already honors XDG env vars on Windows.**
The bundled sidecar (`out/main/chunks/node-*.js`) uses standard xdg-basedir logic:

```js
xdgData   = env.XDG_DATA_HOME   || join(home, ".local", "share")
xdgConfig = env.XDG_CONFIG_HOME || join(home, ".config")
xdgCache  = env.XDG_CACHE_HOME  || join(home, ".cache")
xdgState  = env.XDG_STATE_HOME  || join(home, ".local", "state")
```

So `opencode.db`, auth.json, config, agents, plugins, rg.exe and models.json all follow these four variables — no code change needed on the engine side. (The in-tree `TEST_ONBOARDING` mode already redirects exactly these plus userData to a tmp root, so there's precedent.)

**2. The only missing piece is Electron's userData.**
In `out/main/index.js`:

```js
app.setPath("userData", join(app.getPath("appData"), appId)); // = %APPDATA%\ai.opencode.desktop
```

Two gotchas I hit:
- `--user-data-dir` does **not** help — the explicit `setPath()` overrides it.
- Overriding the `APPDATA` env var also does **not** help — Chromium resolves Roaming AppData via the registry (`SHGetKnownFolder`), not the environment.

So userData needs an actual code hook. Minimal change:

```js
app.setPath("userData",
  process.env.OPENCODE_USER_DATA || join(app.getPath("appData"), appId));
```

**3. Everything else is already env-var friendly.**
- Updater cache (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\<appId>-updater`) follows `LOCALAPPDATA`.
- The sidecar is an in-process Electron utility (no external Node/Bun), so nothing else escapes the process environment.
- No asar-integrity fuses are enabled in the shipped exe, and the single-instance lock is keyed on userData — a portable instance with its own profile runs fine **alongside** the installed one (verified).

### Proposed implementation

A launcher script makes the whole folder movable:

```bat
@echo off
setlocal
set "ROOT=%~dp0"
set "XDG_DATA_HOME=%ROOT%data\opencode-data"
set "XDG_CONFIG_HOME=%ROOT%data\opencode-config"
set "XDG_CACHE_HOME=%ROOT%data\opencode-cache"
set "XDG_STATE_HOME=%ROOT%data\opencode-state"
set "OPENCODE_USER_DATA=%ROOT%data\desktop"
start "" "%ROOT%\OpenCode.exe"
endlocal
```

Even better (and matching the `OPENCODE_PORTABLE_HOME` suggestion in this issue): support a **single** variable that the app expands internally, so users don't need to know about XDG at all:

```js
// main process
const portableHome = process.env.OPENCODE_PORTABLE_HOME;
if (portableHome) {
  for (const [k, sub] of Object.entries({
    XDG_DATA_HOME: "data", XDG_CONFIG_HOME: "config",
    XDG_CACHE_HOME: "cache", XDG_STATE_HOME: "state",
  })) process.env[k] ??= join(portableHome, sub);
}
app.setPath("userData", portableHome ? join(portableHome, "desktop") : /* existing */);
```

Then the launcher is one `set` + a start. (I verified the multi-variable variant end-to-end: 3.2 GB tree on a USB-style path, running in parallel with an installed instance, all state — including the SQLite db and engine logs — landing next to the exe.)

### Edge cases worth deciding for an official build

- **Auto-updater**: with env redirection the updater cache moves into the portable folder and NSIS in-place updates replace files next to the exe (works). Still, consider a flag to disable auto-update or switch to zip-based updates in portable mode, as requested.
- **Deep links**: `opencode://` is registered by the installer pointing at the install path; in portable mode it should be registered per-machine on first launch (HKCU) or via an explicit option.
- **Air-gapped first run**: the engine downloads rg.exe + models.json into `XDG_CACHE_HOME/opencode` — fine for USB use, but worth documenting that pre-seeding that folder makes first run offline-capable.

Following the branch audits, the cache bound was reverted in `4551204c` before merge: LRU eviction by load time can dispose an instance a long-running session still holds (no refcount), load awaiters are unprotected during concurrent eviction, a reload racing `disposeContext` can destroy the new generation's resources, and eviction can lead to a double dispose.

Requirements for re-landing: (1) in-use guard or refcount around `provide`, (2) awaiter protection during eviction, (3) serialize dispose vs reload per directory, (4) fix the double-dispose after eviction, (5) regression tests covering all four.

We're reverting the cache bound for now based on a full audit: evicting a completed entry can dispose a directory that is still in use (a long-running session holds the context without re-touching the store; once more than a bound's worth of directories have been loaded, the next load evicts it mid-flight), and the dispose path races `reload()` (async disposers can run against a freshly swapped entry, and a second identity guard can leave a dead cached entry).

To re-land safely it needs: an in-use refcount or lease around `provide()` and load awaiters, serialization between dispose and reload per directory, a double-dispose guard, and tests that evict while a borrower is active.
